marketReports.title: The State of Data Downtime, 2026
marketReports.summary: Data incidents are getting more frequent and more expensive as stacks get more complex, but most teams still detect issues reactively — from a Slack complaint, not a monitor.

sections.heading: Why this matters now
sections.body:
As companies adopt modern data stacks (Snowflake/BigQuery + dbt + orchestration), pipeline complexity has grown faster than the tooling teams use to monitor it. The result: more failure points, and less visibility into any single one of them.

This creates a specific, recurring buying trigger — a bad-data incident that reaches leadership — which is the single strongest signal for outbound and inbound alike.

sections.heading: What's driving urgency
sections.body:
- Modern data stack adoption continues to accelerate among Series B+ SaaS companies
- Data teams are growing headcount faster than they're growing tooling maturity, widening the observability gap
- Executive dashboards are increasingly tied to board reporting, raising the cost of a bad number reaching a board deck

sections.heading: Buying implication
sections.body: Deals move fastest when triggered by a recent, specific incident. Discovery should always probe for 'tell me about the last time a bad number made it to a dashboard or a deck' — the answer usually reveals both the pain and the internal champion.

battlecards.positioningStatement: MonteGuard is built for large, mature data teams with dedicated platform headcount to configure and maintain it. Northwind is built to be useful on day one for lean teams — anomaly detection and lineage work out of the box, without a multi-week implementation.

competitor.name: MonteGuard
competitor.oneLiner: Enterprise data observability platform, strong in large-scale anomaly detection.
strengths: Strong brand recognition among enterprise data teams
weaknesses: Long implementation (often 4-8 weeks to real value)
Pricing scales aggressively with data volume, punishing growth
Requires dedicated ownership to tune and maintain
competitor.pricingNotes: Typically priced on data volume/table count; costs escalate quickly for fast-growing data estates. Enterprise contracts, annual commit expected.
whenTheyWin: Buyer has a dedicated, well-staffed data platform team (5+ people) with time to own the tool
Enterprise buyer with existing budget and a mandate for a 'best of breed' name
whenWeWin: Lean data team (1-10 people) that needs value fast without a dedicated observability owner
Budget-conscious buyer who needs predictable pricing as data volume grows
Team already using dbt and wants observability that fits that workflow natively
landmines: Ask: 'Who on your team will own tuning MonteGuard's anomaly thresholds week to week?'
Ask: 'What happens to your MonteGuard bill when your data volume doubles next year?'
proofPoints: Customers report going live with meaningful monitoring coverage inside the first week
Predictable, seat-and-scope based pricing rather than pure volume-based pricing

talkTrack: Open by acknowledging MonteGuard is a credible, well-known name — don't trash it.
Ask how big the team is that would own the tool day-to-day; surface the staffing gap if it's small.
Reframe the decision from 'most powerful platform' to 'fastest path to a team actually trusting its data again.'
Anchor on time-to-value: what would go live in week one versus week six.
Close by offering a scoped pilot on their actual highest-risk pipeline.
doNotSay: Don't claim feature parity on advanced anomaly detection — MonteGuard is genuinely stronger there for large, mature use cases.
Don't disparage MonteGuard's brand or customers directly.
battleTestedQuotes: "We're not trying to out-enterprise MonteGuard — we're trying to get your team to trust its data by next Friday, not next quarter."

objections.objection: This feels expensive for where we are right now.
objections.underlyingConcern: They can't yet tie the cost to an avoided incident, or they're worried about justifying a new line item internally.
objections.response: Ask them to put a number on the last data incident: how long it took to catch, how many people got pulled in, and what it cost in trust with the exec team or a customer. Anchor the price against that, not against a hypothetical budget line.
followUpQuestions: What did the last bad-data incident actually cost you — in time, in trust, or in a customer relationship?
If this tool had caught that issue in minutes instead of a stakeholder complaint, what would that have been worth?
supportingProof: Median time-to-detect without observability tooling runs around 4 hours, often triggered by a stakeholder complaint rather than a monitor.

objections.objection: Can't we just build this with dbt tests and some Slack alerts?
objections.underlyingConcern: They've already invested effort in a DIY solution and are worried about sunk cost or looking like they can't build it themselves.
objections.response: Validate that dbt tests are a great start — and explain that they cover known failure modes, not unknown ones (schema drift, freshness, volume anomalies you didn't think to test for). Position Northwind as the layer that catches what you didn't know to check for, not a replacement for good dbt hygiene.
followUpQuestions: How many dbt tests are you maintaining today, and who owns writing new ones as the pipeline grows?
What's caught the last few incidents — a test you wrote in advance, or someone noticing something looked off?
supportingProof: Most incidents reported by prospects were the kind no one had written a test for in advance — schema changes, silent volume drops, stale data.

objections.objection: Data quality isn't a top priority for us this quarter.
objections.underlyingConcern: No recent painful incident has made this visible/urgent yet, or it's being deprioritized against feature work.
objections.response: Don't push — ask what would need to happen for it to become a priority, and plant a flag: offer to be the call they make when (not if) a data incident happens. Leave them with the market report as a credibility-building resource in the meantime.
followUpQuestions: What would have to happen for this to move up the list?
Who finds out first today when a dashboard number is wrong?
supportingProof: The State of Data Downtime, 2026 report — useful as a low-pressure follow-up resource.
